title: Journey 3: A Chain Reorders by EDI, From Order to Invoice
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/39-journey-wholesale-order/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (the contrast with Journeys 1 and 2, the thesis and roadmap paragraphs, the reading paragraph of the January table and the conclusion's synthesis); these are listed under decision_log.

know: The six EDI messages of one wholesale order (ORDERS, CONTRL, ORDRSP, DESADV, INVOIC, RECADV) with the system each is generated from, the three GS1 identifiers (GTIN, GLN, SSCC), and the fifteen steps from the order message to cash application.

Bergzicht's spring reorder in the late-2027 design: ORDERS on 6 April 2027 for 240 units across 18 SKUs, €19,860 excluding VAT; validation of items, contract prices and credit against the ERP; allocation in the availability service; three pallets with SSCC labels from the WMS at pack; the DESADV from the pack confirmation before the pallets leave; delivery to Zwolle and the INVOIC on 9 April (€24,030.60 gross); payment due 9 May as a SEPA transfer to be matched.

The ASN Chargeback of Q3 2026 (€14,200: despatch advices generated by the ERP at release with ERP pallet numbers while the WMS printed its own labels), why it went unseen for a quarter, W6's rules, and the Peppol variant for Ardennes Trail Co. (40 jackets, €3,800, ordered 21 April 2027, invoiced 23 April, due 23 May).
believe: Each wholesale document is a promise in the buyer's contract, usually with a penalty.
The despatch advice must be written by the system that packed the pallets.
E-invoicing mandates change an invoice's format and transport, not its owner.
can_do: Say, for each document in their own wholesale flow, which system generates it and whether that system saw the fact it states.
Keep a partner card per trading partner (GLNs, guideline version, messages, test status, contacts, an owner) and detect deductions as cases with evidence.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture, in particular anyone who meets EDI for the first time as a wall of capital letters: the integration engineer handed a trading-partner guideline, the product manager asked why a deduction appeared, the finance analyst matching a short payment.
already_knows: Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 and January 2027 incidents in outline (including the ASN Chargeback by name) and the names of the sixteen failure patterns.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' and 'commerce platform', business models and the four scale stages, the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II and III: product, variant, SKU and GTIN; prices frozen at order placement; available-to-promise and per-channel buffers; one order record; one invoice per shipment, credit notes as the only correction, the monthly match of invoices, payouts and bank lines.
From Part IX so far: Journey 1 (Eva's order #1072455 of 13 April 2027 replayed through the late-2027 design, the step table and handoff requirements) and Journey 2 (its return and exchange).
does_not_know: The EDI messages ORDERS, CONTRL, ORDRSP, DESADV, INVOIC, RECADV; the GLN and the SSCC; VAN and AS2; a message implementation guideline, mapping and the partner card.

Allocation for a wholesale order; the four-way match; payment terms, receivable, cash application, dunning; Peppol, access point, the four-corner model, EN 16931, UBL, BIS Billing 3.0; intra-EU supply with reverse charge and VIES.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given deductions for mismatched pallets, the reader names the despatch advice's source as the cause and the system that should write it, rather than blaming the warehouse or the EDI provider.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A supplier's ERP sends a retail chain's despatch advice when it releases an order to the warehouse, numbering the pallets itself; the warehouse system prints its own pallet labels at packing. Months later the chain's payments arrive short, with deduction codes, on invoices that are correct. Using only this chapter: what is wrong, why did nobody notice, and what should change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The despatch advice described the order, while the pallets described the pack, so the chain's receiving scanned SSCCs that were missing from the notice or carried different contents, counted by hand and charged fees under its purchasing conditions. Nobody noticed because the deductions arrived as unexplained short payments: finance saw receivables that did not close, the wholesale lead heard of 'label problems', the warehouse had shipped every unit, and only one external consultant could read the mapping. The system that packs the pallet should print the SSCC and write the despatch advice from its pack confirmation, sent before the truck leaves (the truck waits if not); a partner card names the guideline version, the change contact and an owner; a compliance scorecard and an alarm on negative acknowledgements watch it; and a short payment opens a case with the invoice, the despatch advice and the deduction code as evidence.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say where an EDI order should become an order record and what protects that step.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An EDI order arrives, the network redelivers it an hour later, two lines carry prices that differ from the contract, and the team's habit is to key EDI orders into the EDI provider's web portal and the ERP. Using only this chapter: what should happen to this order, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A syntax acknowledgement (CONTRL) says only that the message parsed, not that it was accepted. The order is validated against data the ERP owns (each GTIN resolves to a SKU, prices equal the customer's contract prices, open receivables within the credit limit), and the price mismatch is answered in the order response (ORDRSP), never silently accepted, because an unexpected invoice price becomes a short payment. The order is created once, in the OMS, with channel EDI, the same number family and state model as web orders, keyed on the buyer's GLN plus its PO number, so the redelivered copy does nothing; not in the portal or the ERP. The allocation is committed in the availability service, so every channel's available stock drops within seconds.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what an e-invoicing mandate changes in the invoice flow and what it does not.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch supplier's Belgian business customer stops accepting PDF invoices. Using only this chapter: what changes in the supplier's invoicing, what stays the same, and is the supplier obliged?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The invoice is still issued by the ERP from what shipped. Its format becomes a Peppol BIS Billing 3.0 invoice (UBL implementing EN 16931) sent through the supplier's access point to the customer's in the four-corner model, at 0% as an intra-EU supply with the reverse-charge mention once the customer's VAT number is validated in VIES; transmission becomes a state the ERP holds (sent, delivered, rejected), and a rejected e-invoice is not an invoice. Belgium has required structured e-invoices between Belgian businesses since 1 January 2026; whether that reaches a Dutch supplier without a Belgian establishment is not settled by the chapter's sources, but the customer's bookkeeping expects Peppol either way. Germany requires businesses to receive e-invoices since 2025, the Netherlands plans a mandate for 2030 and ViDA brings cross-border digital reporting from July 2030.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a retail chain ordering pallets expects its receiving system to recognize what arrives, so the supplier's shipment notice and pallet labels must match and a correct delivery can still be held up or penalized when they disagree; that EDI carries orders, shipment notices and invoices; that a wholesale order is a conversation of documents with a contract behind it, each with its own system of truth, and that Kestrel & Pine lost €14,200 because its despatch advices came from the wrong system; that money arrives as a bank transfer to match and e-invoicing changes format and transport, not owner; that wholesale is a quarter of Kestrel & Pine's revenue from 1,100 accounts with orders about fourteen times larger; that Bergzicht's order commits 240 units on 6 April from the stock Eva buys from on 13 April; and that the walk runs from receipt to payment. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's reorder and the ASN Chargeback, GS1 standards, retailers' published conditions (Jumbo, bol, Walmart), EDI and Peppol providers and Belgian, German and EU e-invoicing rules.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: How does a wholesale reorder by EDI run from order to invoice, and where does it fail?
thesis.claim: A wholesale reorder runs as a chain of documents, each a contractual promise: the order message becomes one order record in the OMS, keyed on the buyer's location number and purchase-order number; the warehouse system writes the despatch advice from the pallets as packed; the ERP writes the invoice from the shipped lines; and the money arrives thirty days later as a bank transfer to match. It fails where a document is written by a system that did not see the fact it states.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that EDI is a translation job owned by an EDI provider or a consultant: map the ERP's order to the retailer's format, generate the despatch advice and the invoice from the order, and treat deductions as a finance matter.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim asks, for each document, which system generates it and whether that system touched the goods, keeps one partner card per trading partner with an owner, and treats every short payment as a case with evidence. In Q3 2026 Kestrel & Pine's ERP generated Bergzicht's despatch advices at release, with its own pallet numbers, while the WMS printed different labels at pack; nine deliveries produced €14,200 in deductions, unseen for a quarter because they arrived as short payments on correct invoices and only an external consultant could read the mapping. Under W6, Waypoint's EDI rule, the WMS prints the SSCC at pack and sends the despatch advice from its pack confirmation, and Bergzicht's 6 April 2027 reorder (240 units, €19,860) arrives on 9 April with a matching notice and is invoiced that day for €24,030.60, due 9 May. For Ardennes Trail Co. in Namur the same ERP invoice travels over Peppol: the format and transport change, the owner does not.
thesis.how_why: The buyer's receiving scans each pallet's SSCC and books the contents listed for it in the despatch advice without counting, and its four-way match of order, despatch advice, receipt and invoice pays short whatever disagrees, under purchasing conditions with fees per message and per refused delivery (Jumbo's, for example). Only the system that built a pallet knows what is on it, so a notice written from the order states what should have shipped, not what did. Networks redeliver messages and buyers resend after timeouts, so the order record needs the GLN and PO number as its key; contract prices and credit limits live in the ERP, so validation reads them there; and an issued invoice is immutable, so it is written from the shipped lines.

supporting_claims.claim: A wholesale order is a chain of documents (order, order response, despatch advice, invoice), each a promise in the buyer's purchasing conditions with a penalty behind it, tied together by three GS1 identifiers: the GTIN for the item, the GLN for the location and the SSCC for the pallet.

The order message becomes one order record in the OMS, validated against the items, contract prices and credit limit the ERP owns and keyed on the buyer's GLN plus PO number so that a redelivered message does nothing, and its stock is committed in the availability service so every channel sees it within seconds.

The despatch advice must be written by the warehouse system from the pallets as packed (the SSCC printed at pack, the DESADV sent from the pack confirmation before the truck leaves), because only the system that built a pallet knows what is on it and the buyer's receiving books what the notice says without counting.

The invoice is the ERP's, written once from the shipped lines, and the money arrives thirty days later as a bank transfer that must be matched to invoices; an e-invoicing mandate changes the invoice's format and transport, not its owner.

On the January 2027 landscape the ERP wrote the despatch advice at release while the WMS printed its own labels, and €14,200 of deductions in Q3 2026 went unseen for a quarter; wholesale fails where a document is written by a system that did not see the fact it states, and it is caught by a partner card, a compliance scorecard and a case per short payment.

role.contribution: Walks Bergzicht's EDI reorder from the order message to the matched bank transfer through the late-2027 design with W6 in force, tells the ASN Chargeback as the failure path, runs a Belgian customer's Peppol invoice as the variant and compares the January 2027 path.

additional_patterns.applies_to: handoffs, january, chargeback, wrong: the walk read back as requirements, a comparison and the failures

flow.rationale: The order, its documents and the step table come first because every step refers to them; the sections then walk the reorder in the order it lives (message in, allocation, packing and despatch advice, invoice and money). Only after the reader has seen every document written do the later sections read the walk back: what each handoff requires, the same order on the January 2027 landscape, the ASN Chargeback that landscape produced, and further failures. The Peppol variant follows the invoice section because it varies that step; placed later it would interrupt the despatch-advice thread that runs from the handoff table's DESADV row to the chargeback. Putting the chargeback before the walk would explain a failure of a document the reader has not seen written; putting it before the January comparison would describe a failure on a landscape the reader has not been shown; putting the January comparison first would contrast a design the reader has not seen work; and the chargeback and the further failures sit together so the failure material is read in one place, just before the conclusion that calls back to it.

hook.content: A retail chain orders pallets of clothing and expects its receiving system to recognize what arrives. The supplier must send the shipment notice in the agreed format and label the pallets so they match it. A correct physical delivery can still be held up or penalized when those records disagree.

bridge.to_topic: The documents that travel with it between two companies' systems, which decide whether that delivery is received and paid; at Kestrel & Pine a quarter of revenue moves this way.

sections.heading: The Order, the Setting and the Rules of This Walk

sections.heading: Allocation: Whose Stock Is It?

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A wholesale order takes stock differently from a web order: Bergzicht's 240 units are allocated three days before they ship while the storefronts, marketplaces and B2B portal keep selling from the same shelves.

In the target design the availability service computes available-to-promise per channel from the WMS's stock events (W1), so the commitment shows everywhere within seconds: 36 moss M jackets on hand, 12 to Bergzicht and one buffer leave 23 for Eva's storefront, while in January 2027 the ERP's order reached the platform an hour later at best.

sections.heading: Pick to Pallet, Label and Despatch Advice: The Document That Costs Money
sections.controlling_idea: The WMS prints each pallet's SSCC at pack and writes the DESADV from that record before the truck leaves, because the buyer's receiving trusts the notice and its contract charges when it is wrong.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the despatch advice written by the system that packed the pallets, and the buyer rules that make it a priced promise.

flow.rationale: The goods move from fulfillment order to pack to notice; the buyer's rules come at the moment the notice is sent, because that is when they bind; the arrival at Zwolle closes the physical journey. Putting the rules before packing would explain a penalty before the reader has seen what it is charged for.

transition_in.introduces: The instruction to ship it and the packing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On Tuesday afternoon the OMS sends the WMS a fulfillment order at the wholesale service level, and Duiven runs the wholesale wave after the morning's parcel waves.

evidence.what: Manhattan: its warehouse product handles 'wholesale, retail, and direct orders at the same time'.
evidence.shows: Parcel and pallet work run side by side in one warehouse system.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Packing is the moment of truth: as each pallet is closed the WMS prints its SSCC and records which cartons and GTINs are on it, W6's first rule, so the label describes the pallet as built, not the order.

transition_in.introduces: The pallets being built and labelled.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The DESADV is written from that record at pack confirmation on Thursday 8 April and reaches Bergzicht before the pallets leave Duiven, W6's second rule: sent from the WMS's confirmation, not from the ERP.

evidence.what: DESADV at pack confirmation, Thursday 8 April (illustrative day), before the pallets leave.
evidence.shows: The notice comes from the same record as the labels.

transition_in.introduces: The notice written from it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Jumbo's published rules show why the buyer cares and what it costs: every delivery must be preceded by a DESADV, one without it is refused, the SSCC label links pallet and message, and its purchasing conditions forfeit €70 per non-compliant message and charge €250 per order line delivered less than 90% on time and in full.

evidence.what: Jumbo DC guidelines (October 2025, translated): 'Every delivery to our mechanized DC must be preceded by a DESADV message'; 'A delivery without an accompanying DESADV message cannot be processed and is therefore refused!'; 'The SSCC label forms the link with the DESADV despatch message'.
evidence.shows: A real buyer treats the notice as a condition of receipt.

evidence.what: Jumbo purchasing conditions, 9 April 2026 (translated): €70 per message, refusal, €250 per order line.
evidence.shows: The notice is a priced promise.

transition_in.carries_over: The notice sent before the truck.
transition_in.introduces: Why the buyer insists on it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: bol has required SSCC labels on every logistic unit since 31 December 2021 and Walmart's on-time-in-full program carried a 3% fee at its 2017 introduction; Bergzicht's conditions are fictional and take this shape.

evidence.what: bol SSCC page (accessed 2026-11); Talk Business & Politics, 2017.
evidence.shows: The rule is common across retailers, not one chain's quirk.

transition_in.introduces: Two more retailers with the same shape.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pallets reach Zwolle on Friday 9 April, where receiving scans each SSCC, finds it in the DESADV and books the contents without counting; Bergzicht sends no RECADV, so the only evidence of receipt is what is not deducted.

evidence.what: Delivered 9 April; Bergzicht sends no RECADV.
evidence.shows: What the buyer's receiving does with the notice.

transition_in.carries_over: The buyer's rules for a notice.
transition_in.introduces: The delivery those rules apply to.

sections.heading: Invoice, Terms and the Money Thirty Days Later
sections.controlling_idea: The ERP invoices from the shipped lines, the buyer matches it against order, notice and receipt, and the money arrives thirty days later as a bank transfer that cash application must match.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the invoice's owner and the money as a receivable to match, not a payment event.

flow.rationale: Invoice, the buyer's match, the books, then the transfer and its matching follow the calendar from 9 April to 9 May; the four-way match must come before the money because it decides what is paid.

transition_in.introduces: The invoice for what was delivered.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The invoice is the ERP's and is written from what shipped: on Friday the ERP issues the INVOIC for €19,860 net, €4,170.60 VAT and €24,030.60 gross, due 9 May, with the legally required contents, immutable once issued and corrected only by credit note.

evidence.shows: The invoice's amounts.

evidence.what: Odoo 18.0: a credit note 'is the only legal method for canceling, refunding, or modifying a validated invoice'.
evidence.shows: Why the invoice must be right when issued.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On Bergzicht's side the invoice meets the four-way match of purchase order, despatch advice, receipt scan and invoice, and any line that disagrees is paid short with a deduction code.

transition_in.carries_over: An invoice written from the shipped lines.
transition_in.introduces: What the buyer does with it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ERP posts a receivable of €24,030.60 and revenue of €19,860 at delivery on 9 April under IFRS 15, so for thirty days Kestrel & Pine carries Bergzicht's credit risk.

evidence.what: IFRS 15, effective 2018: revenue when control passes.
evidence.shows: Revenue at delivery, not at order or payment.

transition_in.introduces: The seller's books.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The money arrives by SEPA transfer with remittance information, possibly in seconds since instant transfers became mandatory in October 2025, and the work is cash application, with reminders and an order hold the OMS must show when payment is late.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2024/886 on instant credit transfers.
evidence.shows: Speed of transfer is not the problem; matching is.

evidence.what: Figure 4: each wholesale document has its own system of truth.
evidence.shows: Summarizes the owners of order, notice, invoice and money.

transition_in.introduces: The day the money comes back.

sections.heading: The Variant: A Belgian Shop's Peppol Invoice
sections.controlling_idea: A Belgian shop's order invoiced over Peppol shows that an e-invoicing mandate changes the invoice's format, VAT treatment and transport, and adds a transmission state, while the ERP stays its owner.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the invoice's owner holds under a different format and network.

flow.rationale: The order, then the Belgian rule, then what Peppol is, then what the ERP produces and how it differs from EDI, then the neighbouring countries; the comparison table needs Peppol explained first.

transition_in.carries_over: Bergzicht's EDI invoice and the money that settles it.
transition_in.introduces: A variant of the invoice step: a small business customer whose invoice travels over Peppol.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ardennes Trail Co., a fictional shop in Namur, orders 40 Ridgewalker jackets at €95 through the B2B portal on 21 April 2027 for €3,800, shipped by bpost and invoiced on 23 April, due 23 May; up to the invoice it is Eva's journey with a company account and terms.

evidence.what: 40 jackets, €3,800, 21 April, 23 April, 23 May.
evidence.shows: The variant's order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Belgium has required structured e-invoices over Peppol between Belgian businesses since 1 January 2026, with fines and a tolerance period but no postponement; whether it reaches a Dutch supplier without a Belgian establishment is not settled by the sources read, and Kestrel & Pine sends Peppol invoices to all Belgian business customers either way.

evidence.what: einvoice.belgium.be (18 September 2024): 'Sending a PDF invoice by e-mail or via a platform will no longer be enough'; fines of €1,500, €3,000 and €5,000; tolerance announced December 2025.
evidence.shows: The rule and its enforcement.

transition_in.introduces: The Belgian rule for its invoices.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Peppol is an open network and document standard: each company connects through an access point in a four-corner model, and the document is a BIS Billing 3.0 invoice in UBL implementing EN 16931.

evidence.what: OpenPeppol; BIS Billing 3.0.21, published 20 May 2026, mandatory 17 August 2026; type codes 380 and 381.
evidence.shows: The network and format named precisely.

transition_in.introduces: What Peppol is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ERP produces the same invoice in substance, differing in VAT (0% intra-EU supply with reverse charge after a VIES check) and transport (through the access points), and transmission becomes a state of the invoice the ERP must hold.

evidence.what: EDI INVOIC to Bergzicht versus Peppol invoice to Ardennes Trail: content, purpose, addressing, transport, validation, legal position in November 2026.
evidence.shows: Format and transport differ; the owner does not.

transition_in.introduces: What the ERP's invoice becomes on it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Germany requires businesses to receive e-invoices since 2025 and tolerates EDI through 2027, ViDA brings cross-border digital reporting from July 2030, and through all of it the invoice's owner stays the same while its format and delivery receipt change.

evidence.what: German BMF FAQ; European Commission ViDA page (adopted 11 March 2025).
evidence.shows: The calendar beyond Belgium.

transition_in.introduces: The neighbouring rules, and what they all leave unchanged.

sections.heading: What Each Handoff Requires
sections.controlling_idea: Read against freshness, consistency, latency and availability, wholesale's handoffs are slower than the consumer journey's but stricter on consistency, and the DESADV handoff tolerates no failure but holding the truck.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the walk into a specification of each join, and singles out the despatch advice.

transition_in.carries_over: Bergzicht's walk from message to money, and the invoice variant.
transition_in.introduces: The joins of Bergzicht's order, specified.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four questions asked of every join give wholesale a different profile from the consumer journey: slower almost everywhere, stricter on consistency, with one hard deadline, the truck.

evidence.what: Seven handoffs from ORDERS in to the bank, with freshness, consistency, latency, availability and style (W5); latencies illustrative.
evidence.shows: Specifies each join and which may be a batch.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The DESADV row is the one with no tolerance: freshness, consistency and the deadline bind at once, and the only safe failure is to hold the truck.

transition_in.introduces: The one that tolerates nothing.

sections.heading: The Same Order in January 2027
sections.controlling_idea: On the January 2027 landscape, where the reorder actually ran, the same systems held the order in the ERP, committed stock an hour late and wrote the despatch advice at release; what changes in the late-2027 design is who writes each document.

advances_thesis.how: Holds the systems constant and shows that the differences are owners and joins.

transition_in.carries_over: The late-2027 handoffs, with the DESADV row that tolerates nothing.
transition_in.introduces: The landscape the April order really ran on, which had run through 2026.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In April 2027 the reorder actually ran on the January landscape with the same ERP, WMS and EDI provider, and side by side the two paths differ in where the order lives, who can read the mapping, how fast stock is committed, which system writes the despatch advice and from what the invoice is written.

evidence.what: Late 2027 versus January 2027: where the order lives, who reads the mapping, stock, SSCC and DESADV, invoice, deductions.
evidence.shows: The same systems with different owners and joins.

sections.heading: The Failure Path: The ASN Chargeback
sections.controlling_idea: In Q3 2026 the ERP wrote despatch advices at release while the WMS printed its own labels, costing €14,200 unseen for a quarter; W6 supplies the detection and the evidence that were missing, and names what can still go wrong.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the failure the despatch-advice rule prevents, why it stayed hidden, and how it is caught now.

flow.rationale: Mechanism, consequence, why it was unseen, then detection, recovery and residual failures: the remedies only make sense against the mechanism and the silence.

transition_in.carries_over: The January landscape, where the ERP wrote the despatch advice at release.
transition_in.introduces: The failure that path produced in Q3 2026.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: That January path produced the ASN Chargeback in the third quarter of 2026, which cost €14,200.

evidence.shows: The incident's size and date.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The old ERP flow generated the DESADV when it released the order to the warehouse, with its own pallet numbers and expected contents, while the WMS packed the actual goods and printed its own labels.

evidence.what: ERP-generated DESADV at release with ERP pallet numbers; WMS labels at pack.
evidence.shows: Two systems wrote two descriptions of one pallet.

transition_in.introduces: Its mechanism.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Bergzicht therefore received pallets whose numbers or contents did not match the notice, or notices after the truck, each forcing a manual count and a contractual fee; nine Q3 deliveries produced the October 2026 deduction.

evidence.what: Nine deliveries; deduction in the October 2026 remittance (illustrative count).
evidence.shows: The mechanism's cost in practice.

transition_in.carries_over: Notice and labels written by different systems.
transition_in.introduces: What the buyer's receiving saw.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Nobody saw it for a quarter because the deductions arrived as unexplained short payments on correct invoices, finance, wholesale and the warehouse each saw one piece, only the consultant could read the mapping (the Lynchpin), and nobody owned the contract's demand for pallet-level content (the Pulled Rug).

transition_in.introduces: Why it stayed invisible.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In the target design three signals replace the silence: a compliance scorecard on the partner card, an alarm on any negative acknowledgement, and a case opened for every short payment naming the invoice, the DESADV and the deduction code.

transition_in.introduces: The signals that detect it now.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A deduction can be disputed only with evidence that the DESADV described the pallets as shipped, which W6 produces; the €14,200 was not disputed because that evidence did not exist.

transition_in.introduces: Recovery.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: W6 still leaves failures to guard against: a DESADV sent after the truck, a negative CONTRL left unread, a quantity changed after sending and a reused SSCC serial, each with its fix.

evidence.what: Figure 5: in January 2027 the despatch advice described the order while the pallets described the pack; after W6 one system writes both.
evidence.shows: The failure as an architecture problem, not a warehouse one.

transition_in.introduces: What can still go wrong after it.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong Along This Path
sections.controlling_idea: Beyond the ASN path, five recurring wholesale failures each have a detection and a recovery, and all reduce to write-off, retry or compensation.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the remaining failures sit at handoffs and are caught by keys, cases and partner cards.

transition_in.carries_over: The ASN path and what can still go wrong after W6.
transition_in.introduces: Five more failures on this path.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Beyond the ASN path, five failures recur in wholesale: the duplicate ORDERS, the change after allocation, the short pick, the remittance that names nothing and the guideline revision are each caught by a key, a re-validation, the shipped quantity, a cash-application rule or the partner card.

evidence.what: A transfer of €23,214.80 against three invoices and two deductions (illustrative).
evidence.shows: What a remittance without invoice numbers looks like.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Hohpe's three recoveries, write-off, retry and compensating action, cover all five; in wholesale the compensation is a credit note and the write-off is a deduction nobody disputed.

evidence.what: Gregor Hohpe, 'Starbucks does not use two-phase commit' (2004).
evidence.shows: A general name for the recoveries.

transition_in.introduces: The three kinds of recovery they reduce to.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The opening's puzzle, a correct delivery penalized, is a document written by the wrong system. Replayed through the late-2027 design, Bergzicht's three pallets arrive with labels and a despatch advice from one pack confirmation, are booked without counting and invoiced from what shipped; in Q3 2026 the same warehouse shipped every unit and Kestrel & Pine still lost €14,200, because the ERP had described the order instead of the pallets. Each wholesale document is safe when the system that saw its fact writes it, and an e-invoice changes the format and transport, not the writer.
conclusion.so_what: A supplier that asks, for each document, which system writes it and whether that system saw the fact, keeps a partner card per buyer and opens a case for every short payment finds its deductions before the buyer's receiving does.

callback.to: The introduction's hook: a retail chain whose receiving system must recognize what arrives, where a correct physical delivery can still be held up or penalized when the records disagree.
callback.how: The reader can now say which record disagreed in Kestrel & Pine's case and which system should have written it.

takeaway.content: List every document you exchange with each trading partner, write next to it the system that generates it and whether that system saw the fact it states, and put each partner on a one-page partner card with an owner.

hand_off.carries_over: The first three journeys' chain of handoffs, walked on an ordinary April week: Bergzicht's pallets and Eva's parcel leaving the same warehouse.
hand_off.introduces: The day that is not ordinary: the same chain at about forty times its normal load on Black Friday 2026, when the handoffs' delays and copies turned into an oversell, and the plan that rehearses the 2027 evening.

transition_in.carries_over: Six failures and the recoveries they reduce to.
transition_in.introduces: What the whole walk shows, set against the opening.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The opening's correct delivery that is penalized turns out to be a document written by the wrong system: in the late-2027 design Bergzicht's pallets, notice and invoice all come from the systems that saw the facts, while in Q3 2026 the same warehouse shipped every unit and €14,200 was lost because the ERP described the order instead of the pallets, so a supplier that asks of each document who writes it and whether that system saw the fact finds its deductions before the buyer does.

evidence.what: The opening's penalized delivery set against the late-2027 walk and the Q3 2026 incident.
evidence.shows: The reader can now name the document and the system at fault.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: EDI between retailers and suppliers is a buyer-defined exchange with penalties in the contract; the GS1 identifiers divide the work and make the SSCC the pallet's only identifier; an invoice is issued once from what was delivered, corrected only by credit note, revenue counts at delivery, and structured e-invoicing is mandatory, required or planned by country.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's answer in one paragraph.
transition_in.introduces: The points it rests on, starting with what the sources establish.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Depends on context: whether EDI orders should enter an OMS or the ERP, whether to use a direct AS2 link or a provider's network, and whether to send Peppol invoices to customers who are not obliged to receive them.

transition_in.introduces: What depends on the merchant's situation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: the despatch advice is the most dangerous document a merchant sends and whatever packs the pallet writes it, and every trading partner belongs on a one-page partner card, since an EDI relationship only a contractor can explain is an outage waiting to happen.

transition_in.introduces: The author's own reading.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eight questions let a reader check their own wholesale flow: who creates the EDI order record, the duplicate key, who prints the SSCC and writes the DESADV, whether it precedes the truck, where each partner's guideline and owner are recorded, how deductions are detected and disputed, whether invoices come from shipped lines, and which e-invoicing obligations apply.

transition_in.introduces: Questions that apply it to the reader's own flow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Bergzicht's pallets and Eva's parcel left the same warehouse in the same April week on a landscape built for an ordinary day; the next journey is the day that is not ordinary, Black Friday 2026, when the Ridgewalker sold out at 19:40 and the storefronts kept selling it for two hours.
